name: Transaxillary breast augmentation

card.summary: A breast implant operation done through a small incision in the armpit, so that implants add breast volume without a scar on the breast itself.
card.aka: armpit approach; TABA; endoscopic transaxillary augmentation
card.note: Surgical procedure with general operative and implant-related risks; performed by licensed surgeons only.

quick.overview:
Transaxillary breast augmentation places a breast implant through an incision in the armpit crease. The implant is guided under the skin to a pocket behind the breast, so the visible result is a fuller chest contour while the breast skin is left without an incision scar.

Surgical reviews describe it as especially popular in East Asia, and report outcomes comparable to the more common inframammary approach when an endoscope is used to give the surgeon a direct view of the pocket. Randomized and comparative trials have looked at endoscopic versus blind techniques and at different pocket planes.
quick.how: It is performed in an operating room under anesthesia by a plastic surgeon. A short armpit incision is made, a pocket is created for the implant (often with an endoscope for visualization), and the implant is placed and the incision closed. Patients choosing it typically do so because they prefer to avoid a scar on the breast; surgeons consider breast shape, the position of the breast crease and implant type when choosing an approach.
quick.risks: As with other breast augmentation approaches, risks include bleeding, infection, implant malposition or asymmetry, capsular contracture and later reoperation. Axillary-specific issues reported in the literature include armpit scarring, bowstring-like cords (Mondor's disease) and possible interaction with later sentinel lymph node mapping for breast cancer. Surgeons differ on how it compares technically with other approaches.

lead: Transaxillary breast augmentation is a method of placing breast implants through an incision in the armpit instead of at the breast crease, around the areola, or at the navel. The implant is tunneled to a pocket beneath the breast, either by blunt dissection or, in modern practice, under direct endoscopic vision [3][4]. It is one of the standard incision choices for breast augmentation alongside the inframammary and periareolar approaches [17].

People choose it to increase breast volume and change chest contour while avoiding a scar on the breast. Plastic surgery reviews describe the axillary route as the preferred or most popular incision among women in parts of East Asia, including Korea, and as a good choice for young patients with an indistinct inframammary fold [1][2].

Research on the technique consists mainly of surgeon-authored reviews, case series and a few randomized trials comparing endoscopic with non-endoscopic technique or comparing pocket planes. Authors who advocate it argue that endoscopic assistance gives control equal to other approaches [4]; other papers discuss specific drawbacks such as axillary trauma and sentinel node mapping [5].

Fuller chest contour with no scar on the breast
angle.text: The implant itself adds breast volume; the armpit route changes where the scar sits. People who choose it do so to keep the incision out of the breast area, where it would show in swimwear or low necklines.

paras: In the transaxillary approach the surgeon makes a short incision in the armpit, tunnels the implant across under the skin and creates a pocket either above or below the pectoral muscle, or in a dual plane. Reviews note that the technique can be done by hand or with an endoscope [17][3].

Endoscopic assistance is described as allowing a bloodless pocket and sharp dissection under direct vision, and Korean and Chinese authors report using textured round or anatomical gel implants and high-position dual-plane techniques with it [1][2].

General surveys list the inframammary approach as giving the surgeon the most access, with a longer scar at the breast crease, and the periareolar approach as a short cut around the areola linked in some reports to higher contracture rates and effects on milk ducts. The transaxillary route avoids breast-skin scarring, and its main technical challenge is placing the implant symmetrically in the intended position [17].

Historically the approach was perceived as offering less technical control. Authors of recent reviews argue that endoscopic assistance lets outcomes match those of the inframammary approach and that concerns about longer operations and higher contracture have been misunderstood [3][4].

A randomized controlled trial in the Aesthetic Surgery Journal compared transaxillary augmentation with and without video-assisted endoscopy in a small group of women [8]. A 2026 randomized trial in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery compared a semiendoscopic video-assisted technique with the blind technique [7]. A prospective randomized comparison examined subglandular, subfascial and submuscular implant placement through the axilla [9].

Case series include a nine-year review of 306 endoscopic transaxillary patients [11] and a comparison of submuscular implants via the inframammary and endoscopic transaxillary routes for safety, complications and satisfaction [10]. A five-year study compared form-stable implants placed periareolarly versus transaxillary [14]. Registered trials include a dual-plane axillary approach assisted by endoscope [15] and a study of anesthesia and recovery quality after transaxillary endoscopic augmentation [16].
General breast augmentation risks include hematoma, seroma, infection, capsular contracture, implant rupture, asymmetry and the need for later revision [17].

Specific to the axillary route, a 2007 review raised that more rigid gel implants could traumatize the armpit and interfere with sentinel node mapping in a later breast cancer [5], while other studies examined lymphatic drainage and sentinel node detection after previous transaxillary implants and reported it feasible [12][13]. A case report with a literature review described Mondor's disease, a self-limiting subcutaneous cord, after transaxillary augmentation [6].

timeline.event: Silicone-gel implants are first used for breast augmentation [17].
Registered trial of dual-plane axillary augmentation assisted by endoscope begins [15].
Korean review describes fully endoscopic transaxillary augmentation as comparable to inframammary results [2].
Randomized trial compares semiendoscopic video-assisted and blind transaxillary techniques [7].
